items.t: Commonwealth Bank stock: Business lending offsets credit strain
Commonwealth Bank stock faces arrears pressure after $2.8bn profit
sum: Commonwealth Bank reported a 2.8 billion Australian dollar first-quarter net profit for the three months ended September 30, 2026, but the quarterly update also pointed to increasing pressure on borrowers. As news.com.au reported on November 11, the result was accompanied by a rise in home loans more than 90 days overdue.

Mortgage arrears increased by seven basis points during the quarter to 0.80 percent of the home-loan book. Commonwealth Bank linked the deterioration to cost-of-living pressure caused by higher inflation and interest rates. The bank also said slower resolution after earlier pauses in late-stage collections activity affected the reported arrears rate.

Demand for new housing finance weakened at the same time. Home-loan applications fell 16 percent quarter-on-quarter, while home lending grew 6.6 percent. Deposits increased by 7.7 percent, and business-loan volumes rose as the bank benefited from stronger activity outside the residential mortgage market.

Operating income rose 3 percent in the quarter, but operating expenses increased at the same rate. The result was therefore broadly stable against the average quarterly profit in the second half of fiscal 2026, even though the bank continued to report a large absolute profit.

Loan impairment expenses totalled 30 million Australian dollars. Commonwealth Bank increased collective provisions by 105 million Australian dollars, while the company said its overall coverage remained adequate. The combination of higher arrears, softer applications and unchanged cost growth keeps credit quality and operating efficiency central to the investment case.

Commonwealth Bank stock traded at 104.33 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 09:30 CET on Friday, November 13, 2026. The quote is a current trading indication rather than a confirmed Xetra closing comparison. The quarterly figures give investors two opposing signals: earnings remain resilient, while mortgage stress and weaker loan demand could weigh on future growth.
Australian bank stocks remain sensitive to household credit conditions as investors assess the broader S&P/ASX 200 market.

items.t: Commonwealth Bank of Australia's profit rises, but home loan applications slide
Commonwealth Bank stock faces record housing downturn forecast
sum: Commonwealth Bank economists have sharply lowered their Australian housing outlook, putting the lender's stock in focus as a broader property correction weighs on household wealth and borrowing conditions. In an analysis published on Tuesday, November 3, Commonwealth Bank senior economist Trent Saunders said national dwelling prices could fall 14% from peak to trough, compared with a 9% decline in the bank's September forecast. The figures were published by CommBank.

CommBank now expects the combined five-capital-city index to decline 15% from its peak. National dwelling values fell 1.2% in October, marking a seventh consecutive monthly decline and leaving prices 6.7% below their March peak, according to the bank's analysis. The five-capital-city index was 8.2% below its March peak.

Sydney remains one of the weakest major markets, while Brisbane and Perth have deteriorated faster in recent months. CommBank raised its projected peak-to-trough decline for both cities to 18%, from about 8% in September. Sydney's forecast moved to 16% from 13%, Melbourne's to 13% from 12%, and Adelaide's to 13% from 8%.

Saunders attributed the deeper revision to a correction that was faster and broader than expected. In his assessment, tight underlying housing supply and demand support remain in place, but excessive optimism had become a more important driver of the previous upswing. Even after the projected falls, Brisbane and Perth would remain above their levels before the recent housing boom.

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% at its November meeting, the fifth increase of 2026. CommBank had assumed a peak of 4.60% when it prepared its September housing forecasts. Saunders estimates that the higher rate path reduces national dwelling price growth in 2027 by 2 percentage points compared with the lower-rate scenario.

The broader economic outlook has also weakened. CommBank expects annual economic growth to slow to 1% by mid-2027, down from a previous forecast of 1.8%, and does not expect growth to return to its trend rate of about 2% until the second half of 2028.

sum: Investing.com -- National Australia Bank shares slumped on Thursday after the lender reported weaker full-year earnings, with higher credit impairment charges and software-related costs weighing on profitability.
Shares fell 7.5% to A$38.08, touching their lowest level since October 12 and sharply underperforming the broader S&P/ASX 200, which was up 1.8% in morning trading.

Cash earnings fell 13.4% to A$6.14 billion for the year ended September 30, missing the Visible Alpha consensus estimate of about A$6.33 billion. Statutory net profit attributable declined 9.1% to A$6.14 billion, below analysts' A$6.45 billion estimate.

Net operating income increased 5.8% to A$22.01 billion, supported by higher lending volumes and improved margins. However, credit impairment charges jumped 85.7% to A$1.55 billion from A$833 million a year earlier, including a A$403 million increase in collective provisions reflecting a more challenging economic outlook.

The bank's cash earnings included A$1.35 billion in large notable items, primarily related to a change in its software capitalisation policy. Excluding these items, cash earnings remained broadly flat at A$7.09 billion, also below analysts' A$7.24 billion estimate on an adjusted basis.
NAB's net interest margin (NIM) improved 6 basis points to 1.80%, as at quarter end.
The increase in credit charges included A$1.08 billion in individually assessed provisions, primarily related to business lending customers.

Why bonds are back on investors’ radars
sum: Australian investors have long looked to dividend-paying shares for income, but higher interest rates are changing the alternatives available to them.
After more than a decade in which low rates reduced the returns available from many fixed income investments, bond yields have risen in 2026, lifting the income available.

The shift has brought an asset class often overlooked by self-directed investors back into focus, Senior Vice President, Global Wealth Management with global bond investment firm PIMCO Kanish Chugh said in a CommSec Executive Series interview.
Chugh said Australian investors had traditionally been comfortable with shares, helped by the income available from dividends and franking credits.
But a long period of unusually low interest rates had also played a role.

“When you think about low interest rate environments that we had for much of the 2010s and early 2020s, we had this environment where Australian investors weren’t getting a high rate of return should they put their cash towards a term deposit, for example,” he said.
Chugh said the bond yields being seen in late 2026 were high compared with much of the period since the Global Financial Crisis, but less unusual when viewed over a longer timeframe.

The S&P/ASX 200 index rose 30.3 points, or 0.34%, to close at 8,886.8 on Melbourne Cup day, recovering part of Monday's 0.6% decline.
The market opened strongly, with the benchmark up 0.43% to 8,894 in the first half hour of trading as gains in mining and industrial stocks lifted the index.
Gains faded around midday, and the index slipped into slightly negative territory, trading at 8,855 at 1:30 p.m. local time amid reports of fresh U.S. strikes on Iran, according to Capital Brief.
The index dipped again briefly when the RBA announced its decision at 2:30 p.m., falling about 0.15% at its session low, before rebounding sharply into the close.

The RBA raised its cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, its fifth increase in 2026 and the highest level since late 2008. The central bank also raised rates in February, March, May and September.
The decision was widely expected. Money markets had priced in about an 80% chance of a hike.

sum: A morning rally for US stocks petered out on Monday as the tech and AI industries remained shaky following their sell-off last week.
The S&P 500 sank 0.5% after erasing a gain that had reached 1.1% early in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 213 points, or 0.4%, while the Nasdaq composite fell 1.1%.

The mixed performance for indexes came even though the majority of stocks within the S&P 500 climbed. They benefited from a 7.6% drop in the price of a barrel of Brent crude to $US104.77. It's the latest yo-yo move for oil prices amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal.

The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $US70 and $US120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began, and it's been quick to reverse direction.

So have stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry, which have been shaky for months amid criticism that they surged too high and are in a bubble. Worries are growing that all the hundreds of billions of dollars Big Tech companies are pouring into AI data centres won't yield enough productivity and profit to make the investments worth it.

The latest profit reports from Alphabet and other Big Tech companies also showed how AI may be dragging on their own businesses. Not only did Google's parent company burn through more cash during the latest quarter, as measured by something called free cash flow, it also reported slower-than-expected growth in its search business, which raised worries about AI undercutting its cash cow. That caused Alphabet's stock to drop more than 12% on Thursday for its worst day on record.

On Monday, Alphabet initially rallied 2.6%, but it later erased the gain and then finished with a loss of 0.3%. Nvidia, meanwhile, went from an early gain of 2.6% to a drop of 1.3% following its 4.2% slide on Friday. Such swings dragged the rest of the market with them.

sum: Shares in Australia’s biggest banks have plummeted as analysts warned the budget’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax rules would weaken housing credit growth, while the Commonwealth Bank’s shares were weighed down by a poorly received trading update.

Investors wiped close to $30 billon off the Commonwealth Bank’s market value, after its shares plunged 10.4 per cent due to a combination of the budget’s changes and quarterly earnings that were weaker than expected.

The slump in the nation’s second-biggest stock weighed down the rest of the market, with the S&P/ASX 200 finishing the session down 40.3 points, or 0.5 per cent, at 8630.40, its fourth consecutive decline. The Australian dollar traded at US72.42¢ at the time the market closed.

CBA’s biggest rivals also fell, albeit less dramatically, with Westpac losing 2.8 per cent, National Australia Bank falling 1.5 per cent and ANZ Bank losing 1.6 per cent. The drop in bank shares came after analysts warned the budget’s policies on housing investment would weigh on lending growth and dampen sentiment towards housing – the largest source of loans for Australian banks. CBA and Westpac are the biggest mortgage lenders.

Morgan Stanley analyst Richard Wiles said the budget’s changes, which included limiting negative gearing and capital gains discounts to newly built properties, would have a “negative impact on housing market sentiment and the mortgage market”. He said the policies implied softer mortgage growth, which would be a “headwind” to bank profits.

“In our view, favourable tax treatment is one of the reasons why there has been a 30-year housing ‘super-cycle’ in Australia. However, changes to property-related tax concessions could have a profound effect on the long-term demand for investment properties,” Wiles said.

The slump came as the market lost ground for the fourth day in a row, as the Middle East war drags on without resolution in sight and financial stocks slumped with CBA, the nation’s biggest bank, plunging after it reported lower-than-expected quarterly profits.

Commonwealth Bank’s H1 earnings hit record on market share gains, shares surge
sum: It has been the standout performer of Australia’s Big Four banks in the past year

[SYDNEY] Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) shares surged by as much as 8.4 per cent on Wednesday (Feb 11), after the country’s largest lender reported record first-half cash earnings on the back of market share gains in home loans, business loans and deposits.
The bank’s ability to further entrench its scale advantage over its Big Four peers offset a small decline in margins – due to competition and lower income from its treasury and markets divisions.

CBA reported a record cash net profit after tax of A$5.5 billion (S$4.9 billion) for the six months ended Dec 31, higher than A$5.1 billion for the corresponding year-ago period, and ahead of the Visible Alpha consensus estimate of A$5.2 billion.
The share price performance was CBA’s biggest intra-day gain since late March 2020, and far outpaced the 1.6 per cent rise in the benchmark S&P/ASX200 index on Wednesday.

“The main highlight from this result from CBA has been the growth in the business bank and operational excellence across mortgages in a higher competition environment,” said Michael Haynes, investment analyst at Atlas Funds Management, which owns CBA shares.
CBA, considered one of the most expensive banks in the world, had been the standout performer of Australia’s Big Four banks in the past year.

sum: The Nasdaq led gains on Wall Street as investors went bargain-hunting in US technology shares beaten down last week.
Stock indexes rose with US technology shares and silver also jumped, as investors returned to risk assets.

Technology shares led gains on Wall Street and the Nasdaq was up the most of the three major US indexes. Software names in particular had been pressured the previous week by concerns that artificial intelligence could intensify competition and squeeze margins.
Stocks in Japan rose to record highs following the resounding election win of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Japan’s Nikkei jumped 3.9 per cent to all-time highs as a decisive majority for the ruling LDP party cleared the way for more spending and tax cuts.
The prospect of increased borrowing pushed two-year Japanese government bond yields to their highest since 1996 at 1.3 per cent.
The yen strengthened sharply, reversing six consecutive days of losses, most notably against the dollar.

Here's the earnings forecast out to 2029 for CBA shares
sum: Owning Commonwealth Bank of Australia (ASX: CBA) shares could come with steady earnings growth in the next few years, according to the projections from leading experts.
Experts regularly describe the ASX bank share as expensive. But, the CBA share price has dropped more than 10% in the past six months, as the chart below shows.
While the CBA share price does have a higher price/earnings (P/E) ratio than other ASX bank shares, it has an impressive record of regularly increasing earnings.
Let's take a look at where earnings are expected to go in the coming years.
The last update investors saw from the ASX bank share was the first quarter of FY26, which saw $2.6 billion of cash net profit, representing a year-over-year increase of 2%.

The update saw CBA's business lending grow by 10% year-over-year, household deposits grow by 9.5% year-over-year and home lending grow by 6.1%. However, operating expenses rose by 4% (excluding restructuring and notable items) because of wage and IT vendor inflation.
CBA's underlying net interest margin (NIM) slightly dropped because of deposit switching, competition and the lower cash rate environment.

ASX closes in the red; CBA, Bendigo shares plunge
sum: The Australian sharemarket closed in negative territory on Tuesday, weighed down by a plunge in Commonwealth Bank shares after the financial giant’s latest update raised questions among investors about the company’s high valuation.

The S&P/ASX 200 fell 17.10 points or 0.2 per cent to 8818.80, with eight of 11 industry sectors in positive territory, but financials were dragged down by CBA, which is the biggest stock on the bourse.

CBA closed 6.6 per cent lower, dropping sharply after it said competition was increasing and its profit margins had fallen in the latest quarter, as it slightly increased market share. While analysts said CBA’s $2.6 billion in quarterly profits were broadly as expected, they also suggested CBA has been priced for near perfection by investors, leaving its share price exposed to potential falls if its numbers did not lead to broker upgrades for the company.

Bendigo and Adelaide Bank shares also tumbled, plunging 8.5 per cent, after a trading update that said unaudited cash earnings in the first quarter were 3.2 per cent below the quarterly average for the June half.
National Australia Bank (down 1.3 per cent) also lost ground, while Westpac (up 1.3 per cent), Macquarie Group (up 0.7 per cent) and ANZ Bank (up 0.5 per cent) all rose.

The miners were mixed, with global mining giant BHP gaining 0.3 per cent, while Rio Tinto and Fortescue Metals both shed 0.2 per cent. Gold miners had more reasons to cheer as the price of the safe haven jumped, with local players Northern Star (up 3.2 per cent) and Evolution Mining (up 1.7 per cent) making solid gains.

Among energy stocks, Ampol rose 1.4 per cent, Woodside Energy added 1.6 per cent, and Santos bounced 2.5 per cent higher. Coal miners Yancoal (down 1 per cent) and Whitehaven Coal (down 2.1 per cent) both lost ground.
